L33: # Four-digit Kaprekar dynamics in odd bases Thanks: Richard E. Schwartz’s research is supported by NSF grant DMS-2505281.
L34: Evan Chen , Ken Ono , Richard E. Schwartz and Dinesh S. Thakur Address: Axiom Math, 124 University Avenue, Palo Alto, CA 94301 Email address: evan@axiommath.ai Email address: ken@axiommath.ai Address: Department of Mathematics, Brown University, Providence, RI 02912 Email address: res@math.brown.edu Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Rochester, Rochester, NY 14627 Email address: dinesh.thakur@rochester.edu
L35: ###### Abstract.
L36: 
L37: Start with four digits, arrange them in both descending and ascending order, subtract, and repeat. This simple process is known as the Kaprekar routine, famous in base ten for sending every nonconstant four-digit string to $6174$. We show that in every odd base $B>3$, the four-digit Kaprekar map has an unexpectedly rigid structure. After at most three iterations, every nonconstant orbit enters an explicit triangular region and on this region the map is conjugate to projective doubling:
L38:  | $$\{[r],[s]\}\longmapsto\{[2r],[2s]\}.$$  |
L39: This gives a complete finite description of all nonconstant terminal cycles, including an explicit formula for their lengths and counts. In particular, the longest terminal cycle has length at most $(B-1)/2$, and equality can occur only when $B$ is prime. For primes $p>5$, equality occurs precisely when the least positive $m$ with $2^{m}\equiv\pm 1\pmod{p}$ is $m=(p-1)/2$. The results proved here were first formulated by Schwartz and Thakur.
L40: As a test case for AI-assisted formal mathematics, AxiomProver produced Lean/mathlib formalizations of these results.
L41: ###### Key words and phrases:
L42: 
L43: Kaprekar dynamics, digit dynamics, finite dynamical systems
L44: 
L45: ###### 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
L46: 
L47: Primary 11A63; Secondary 05A15, 37P99
L48: 
L49: ## 1. Introduction and main results
L50: ### 1.1. Background
L51: 
L52: Kaprekar’s four-digit routine looks, at first, like a numerical magic trick. Take four digits, arrange them in decreasing order, subtract the same digits in increasing order, and repeat. In base ten, the trick is famously dramatic: the process is drawn to the constant $6174$, which is a fixed point since
L53: 
L54:  | $$7641-1467=6174.$$  |
L55: 
L56: For example, starting with the number $2808$, we have the process
L57: 
L58:  | $$2808\longmapsto 8532\longmapsto 6174\longmapsto 6174.$$  |
L59: The surprise is not merely that a fixed point appears, but that a rule made from sorting digits is secretly governed by modular arithmetic. This paper explains that hidden arithmetic for four digits in every odd base.
L60: Kaprekar introduced this routine in his study of decimal digit phenomena [cite21†6 , cite22†7 , cite23†3 ]. In the classical four-digit decimal case, every nonconstant digit string reaches the fixed point $6174$. For 3 decimal digits, the fixed point is $495$. The decimal case, however, is only one member of a larger family. In other bases the four-digit routine need not have a single attracting fixed point.
L61: Its terminal behavior may consist of several cycles, and their lengths depend on the arithmetic of the base.
L62: The generalized Kaprekar problem has been studied from several points of view. In base $10$, fixed points of the Kaprekar map (for every digit length) define the integer sequence OEIS cite24†A099009†oeis.org . Jordan studied self-producing digit sequences [cite25†5 ]. Hasse and Prichett determined the four-digit Kaprekar constants (i.e., fixed points for general bases) [cite26†4 ]. Prichett analyzed five-digit terminating cycles [cite27†10 ].
L63: Thakur developed a broader framework for Kaprekar phenomena in arbitrary bases and digit lengths [cite28†11 ]. Devlin and Zeng studied maximum distances to the four-digit fixed point in the bases where such a fixed point exists [cite29†2 ].
L64: More recently, Yamagami and Matsui developed a detailed theory of $3$-adic Kaprekar loops and obtained formulas for Kaprekar fixed points [cite30†13 , cite31†14 ]. Kay and Downes-Ward extended fixed-point and cycle questions to odd bases using Kaprekar indices and subgroup/coset methods, and their sequel treats even bases, where the classification is more intricate [cite32†8 , cite33†9 ]. Our purpose here is more explicit.
L65: In the four-digit odd-base case, the right coordinates reveal a particularly simple mechanism: after a bounded pre-periodic segment, the Kaprekar map is just projective doubling. The resulting proof is short, but the simplification is quite striking, and gives a transparent route to the cycle-length consequences below while keeping the digit dynamics visible throughout.
L66: ### 1.2. Main classification result
L67: 
L68: Given a $4$-digit positive integer in an odd base $B$, let $a_{1}\geq a_{2}\geq a_{3}\geq a_{4}$ denote its digits in non-increasing order. As noted by Hasse and Prichett [cite26†4 ], the next Kaprekar iterate depends only on the two differences
L69: 
L70: (1)  |  | $$d_{1}=a_{1}-a_{4}\qquad\text{and}\qquad d_{2}=a_{2}-a_{3}.$$  |
L71: 
L72: Thus $d_{1}$ records the outer difference and $d_{2}$ records the inner difference. Accordingly, we define a natural state space
L73: (2)  |  | $$X_{B}\coloneq\{(d_{1},d_{2}):1\leq d_{1}<B,\ 0\leq d_{2}\leq d_{1}\}.$$  |
L74: 
L75: The Kaprekar routine thus induces a map $K_{B}\colon X_{B}\to X_{B}$, sending each difference pair to the next difference pair. Note here we have excluded the trivial case $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}$ by requiring $d_{1}\neq 0$.
L76: In cite10†Section 2 we prove that, after a short pre-periodic segment, these two differences become positive, unequal, and odd; that is, $(d_{1},d_{2})$ will lie in the stable odd region defined by
L77: 
L78: (3)  |  | $$\mathcal{T}_{B}\coloneq\{(d_{1},d_{2})\in X_{B}:d_{1}>d_{2}>0\text{ and }d_{1}\equiv d_{2}\equiv 1\pmod{2}\}.$$  |
L79: We also describe how $K_{B}$ acts on $\mathcal{T}_{B}$. To give this description, rather than working with $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ themselves, we work with their half-sum and half-difference:
L80: 
L81: (4)  |  | $$r=\frac{d_{1}+d_{2}}{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad s=\frac{d_{1}-d_{2}}{2}.$$  |

L39: ###### Abstract.
L40: Given a finitely generated group with generating set $S$, we study the cogrowth sequence, which is the number of words of length $n$ over the alphabet $S$ that are equal to one. This is related to the probability of return for walks the corresponding Cayley graph. Muller and Schupp proved the generating function of the sequence is algebraic when $G$ has a finite-index free subgroup (using a result of Dunwoody).
L41: In this work we make this result effective for free products of finite groups: we determine bounds for the degree and height of the minimal polynomial of the generating function, and determine the minimal polynomial explicitly for some families of free products.
L42: Using these results we are able to prove that a gap theorem holds: if $S$ is a finite symmetric generating set for a group $G$ and if $a_{n}$ denotes the number of words of length $n$ over the alphabet $S$ that are equal to $1$ then $\limsup_{n}a_{n}^{1/n}$ exists and is either $1$, $2$, or at least $2\sqrt{2}$.
L43: ###### Contents
L44:

Introduction
L54: Given a group $G$ with finite generating set $S$ the cogrowth problem considers elements in the free monoid, $S^{*}$, on $S$ whose images in $G$ are equal to the identity; this is a sublanguage of $S^{*}$. We denote the set of these elements by $\mathcal{L}(G;S)$, or simply $\mathcal{L}$ when the context is clear. For many classes of groups the word problem is decidable (i.e., there exists a decision procedure for determining if a word on a set of generators is equal to the identity).
L55: This includes free groups, one-relator groups, polycyclic groups and fundamental groups of closed orientable two-manifolds of genus greater than one. On the other hand, there exist groups with unsolvable word problem, with the first such example being given by Novikov [cite15†16 ].
L56: Here we consider an enumerative version of this problem, in which we are interested in the number of words of a given length in $\mathcal{L}$. This is called the cogrowth function and we denote the number of words of length $n$ by ${\rm CL}(n;G,S)$. The generating function of this counting sequence, $F_{G;S}(t)$, is called the corresponding cogrowth series and is defined
L57: 
L58: (1.1)  |  | $$F(t)=F_{G;S}(t):=\sum_{n\geq 0}{\rm CL}(n;G,S)t^{n}.$$  |
L59: This enumeration problem gives rise to three different notions of complexity. First, there is the complexity of the language $\mathcal{L}(G,S)$, which can be understood using the Chomsky-Schützenberger hierarchy of grammars. Next there is the complexity of the associated generating series, where we regard the class of rational power series as being simplest, with algebraic power series, $D$-finite series, and differentially algebraic series being viewed as increasingly complex classes of power series.
L60: Finally, there is the complexity of the group itself, which is typically understood in terms of desirable group theoretic properties.
L61: When one works at the very simplest level, the three notions of complexity coincide: the language $\mathcal{L}(G,S)$ is a regular language if and only if $G$ is finite [cite16†2 ] and this occurs if and only if $F_{G,S}(t)$ is rational.
L62: Beyond this there are other well known connections: the generating function of an unambiguous context-free language satisfies a polynomial equation and hence is an algebraic power series [cite17†11 , Chapter III], and a result of Muller and Schupp [cite18†14 ] gives that this occurs precisely when $G$ has a finite-index free subgroup (i.e., $G$ is virtually free).
L63: Although, virtually free groups are in some respect complex (e.g., they are non-amenable except in the cyclic-by-finite case), the word problem is relatively straightforward for this class of groups and thus in the sense of complexity of the word problem the class of virtually free groups is “simple”.
L64: While there is a strong overlap between the various notions of complexity (group theoretic, language theoretic, and complexity of power series), there are nevertheless some families of groups which are typically regarded as being structurally well behaved whose corresponding cogrowth series are complex according to our notion of complexity.
L65: For example, it is shown in  [cite19†3 ] that a finitely generated amenable group that is not virtually nilpotent can never have a generating series that satisfies a non-trivial homogeneous linear differential equation with rational function coefficients.

L33: # Four-digit Kaprekar dynamics in odd bases Thanks: Richard E. Schwartz’s research is supported by NSF grant DMS-2505281.
L34: Evan Chen , Ken Ono , Richard E. Schwartz and Dinesh S. Thakur Address: Axiom Math, 124 University Avenue, Palo Alto, CA 94301 Email address: evan@axiommath.ai Email address: ken@axiommath.ai Address: Department of Mathematics, Brown University, Providence, RI 02912 Email address: res@math.brown.edu Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Rochester, Rochester, NY 14627 Email address: dinesh.thakur@rochester.edu
L35: ###### Abstract.
L36: 
L37: Start with four digits, arrange them in both descending and ascending order, subtract, and repeat. This simple process is known as the Kaprekar routine, famous in base ten for sending every nonconstant four-digit string to $6174$. We show that in every odd base $B>3$, the four-digit Kaprekar map has an unexpectedly rigid structure. After at most three iterations, every nonconstant orbit enters an explicit triangular region and on this region the map is conjugate to projective doubling:
L38:  | $$\{[r],[s]\}\longmapsto\{[2r],[2s]\}.$$  |
L39: This gives a complete finite description of all nonconstant terminal cycles, including an explicit formula for their lengths and counts. In particular, the longest terminal cycle has length at most $(B-1)/2$, and equality can occur only when $B$ is prime. For primes $p>5$, equality occurs precisely when the least positive $m$ with $2^{m}\equiv\pm 1\pmod{p}$ is $m=(p-1)/2$. The results proved here were first formulated by Schwartz and Thakur.
L40: As a test case for AI-assisted formal mathematics, AxiomProver produced Lean/mathlib formalizations of these results.
L41: ###### Key words and phrases:
L42: 
L43: Kaprekar dynamics, digit dynamics, finite dynamical systems
L44: 
L45: ###### 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
L46: 
L47: Primary 11A63; Secondary 05A15, 37P99
L48: 
L49: ## 1. Introduction and main results
L50: ### 1.1. Background
L51: 
L52: Kaprekar’s four-digit routine looks, at first, like a numerical magic trick. Take four digits, arrange them in decreasing order, subtract the same digits in increasing order, and repeat. In base ten, the trick is famously dramatic: the process is drawn to the constant $6174$, which is a fixed point since
L53: 
L54:  | $$7641-1467=6174.$$  |
L55: 
L56: For example, starting with the number $2808$, we have the process
L57: 
L58:  | $$2808\longmapsto 8532\longmapsto 6174\longmapsto 6174.$$  |
L59: The surprise is not merely that a fixed point appears, but that a rule made from sorting digits is secretly governed by modular arithmetic. This paper explains that hidden arithmetic for four digits in every odd base.
L60: Kaprekar introduced this routine in his study of decimal digit phenomena [cite21†6 , cite22†7 , cite23†3 ]. In the classical four-digit decimal case, every nonconstant digit string reaches the fixed point $6174$. For 3 decimal digits, the fixed point is $495$. The decimal case, however, is only one member of a larger family. In other bases the four-digit routine need not have a single attracting fixed point.
L61: Its terminal behavior may consist of several cycles, and their lengths depend on the arithmetic of the base.
L62: The generalized Kaprekar problem has been studied from several points of view. In base $10$, fixed points of the Kaprekar map (for every digit length) define the integer sequence OEIS cite24†A099009†oeis.org . Jordan studied self-producing digit sequences [cite25†5 ]. Hasse and Prichett determined the four-digit Kaprekar constants (i.e., fixed points for general bases) [cite26†4 ]. Prichett analyzed five-digit terminating cycles [cite27†10 ].
L63: Thakur developed a broader framework for Kaprekar phenomena in arbitrary bases and digit lengths [cite28†11 ]. Devlin and Zeng studied maximum distances to the four-digit fixed point in the bases where such a fixed point exists [cite29†2 ].
L64: More recently, Yamagami and Matsui developed a detailed theory of $3$-adic Kaprekar loops and obtained formulas for Kaprekar fixed points [cite30†13 , cite31†14 ]. Kay and Downes-Ward extended fixed-point and cycle questions to odd bases using Kaprekar indices and subgroup/coset methods, and their sequel treats even bases, where the classification is more intricate [cite32†8 , cite33†9 ]. Our purpose here is more explicit.
L65: In the four-digit odd-base case, the right coordinates reveal a particularly simple mechanism: after a bounded pre-periodic segment, the Kaprekar map is just projective doubling. The resulting proof is short, but the simplification is quite striking, and gives a transparent route to the cycle-length consequences below while keeping the digit dynamics visible throughout.
L66: ### 1.2. Main classification result
L67: 
L68: Given a $4$-digit positive integer in an odd base $B$, let $a_{1}\geq a_{2}\geq a_{3}\geq a_{4}$ denote its digits in non-increasing order. As noted by Hasse and Prichett [cite26†4 ], the next Kaprekar iterate depends only on the two differences
L69: 
L70: (1)  |  | $$d_{1}=a_{1}-a_{4}\qquad\text{and}\qquad d_{2}=a_{2}-a_{3}.$$  |
L71: 
L72: Thus $d_{1}$ records the outer difference and $d_{2}$ records the inner difference. Accordingly, we define a natural state space
L73: (2)  |  | $$X_{B}\coloneq\{(d_{1},d_{2}):1\leq d_{1}<B,\ 0\leq d_{2}\leq d_{1}\}.$$  |
L74: 
L75: The Kaprekar routine thus induces a map $K_{B}\colon X_{B}\to X_{B}$, sending each difference pair to the next difference pair. Note here we have excluded the trivial case $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}$ by requiring $d_{1}\neq 0$.
L76: In cite10†Section 2 we prove that, after a short pre-periodic segment, these two differences become positive, unequal, and odd; that is, $(d_{1},d_{2})$ will lie in the stable odd region defined by
L77: 
L78: (3)  |  | $$\mathcal{T}_{B}\coloneq\{(d_{1},d_{2})\in X_{B}:d_{1}>d_{2}>0\text{ and }d_{1}\equiv d_{2}\equiv 1\pmod{2}\}.$$  |
L79: We also describe how $K_{B}$ acts on $\mathcal{T}_{B}$. To give this description, rather than working with $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ themselves, we work with their half-sum and half-difference:
L80: 
L81: (4)  |  | $$r=\frac{d_{1}+d_{2}}{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad s=\frac{d_{1}-d_{2}}{2}.$$  |
L82: 
L83: (Note that $r>s>0$, and that $r$ and $s$ are integers because $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$ are odd.)
L84: For pairs $(r,s)$ we pass to projective residue classes modulo $B$, where each residue is identified with its negative. Introduce the notation
L85: 
L86:  | $$P_{B}\coloneq\bigl((\mathbb{Z}/B\mathbb{Z})\setminus\{0\}\bigr)/\{\pm 1\}$$  |
L87: 
L88: for the nonzero projective residue classes. For nonzero $x\in\mathbb{Z}/B\mathbb{Z}$, let $[x]\coloneq\{x,-x\}\in P_{B}$ denote the corresponding residue class in $P_{B}$. Finally, let $\binom{P_{B}}{2}$ denote the (unordered) two-element subsets of $P_{B}$.
L89: We can now state the main structural result.
L90: ###### Theorem 1.1 (Structural classification).
L91: 
L92: Let $B>3$ be odd, and let $K_{B}\colon X_{B}\to X_{B}$ be the four-digit Kaprekar map in difference coordinates. Then $\mathcal{T}_{B}$, as defined in (cite34†3 ), is forward-invariant and
L93: 
L94:  | $$K_{B}^{3}(X_{B})\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{B}.$$  |
L95: 
L96: Moreover, the restricted map $K_{B}\colon\mathcal{T}_{B}\to\mathcal{T}_{B}$ is conjugate to the doubling map
L97: 
L98:  | $$\binom{P_{B}}{2}\to\binom{P_{B}}{2}\quad\text{ by }\quad\{[r],[s]\}\longmapsto\{[2r],[2s]\}$$  |
L99: under the transformation defined in (cite35†4 ).
L100: 
L101: Here, in the context of finite dynamical systems, we explicate the term “conjugate” as follows. Let $f\colon X\to X$ and $g\colon Y\to Y$ be maps. We say that $f$ and $g$ are conjugate under the bijection $\Phi\colon X\to Y$ if
L102: 
L103:  | $$\Phi(f(x))=g(\Phi(x))\qquad\text{for all }x\in X.$$  |
L104: Thus $\Phi$ is a relabeling of the states which turns one system into the other. In the particular case of cite36†Theorem 1.1 , the map $\Phi\colon\mathcal{T}_{B}\to\binom{P_{B}}{2}$ is given by (cite35†4 ), and so cite36†Theorem 1.1 makes an implicit promise that (cite35†4 ) is bijective.
L105: We can thus describe cite36†Theorem 1.1 in English as follows: After at most three iterations, every orbit enters our smaller stable region $\mathcal{T}_{B}$. And on this region $\mathcal{T}_{B}$, the sorting-and-subtracting rule is no longer mysterious! After the change of variables in (cite35†4 ), it is exactly multiplication by $2$, with signs ignored, on unordered pairs of nonzero projective residue classes.
L106: ###### Remark.
L107: 
L108: Here the case $B=3$ needs to be excluded because $\mathcal{T}_{B}$ is empty when $B=3$.
L109: 
L110: ### 1.3. Cycle lengths
L111: 
L112: Clearly, for odd $B$ the doubling map
L113: 
L114:  | $$\binom{P_{B}}{2}\to\binom{P_{B}}{2}\text{ by }\{[r],[s]\}\longmapsto\{[2r],[2s]\}$$  |
L115: 
L116: is bijective. Since conjugate systems have the same cycle lengths, we get the following corollaries as the main consequences. They are stated separately so that the dynamical statement and the arithmetic consequences are easy to distinguish.
L117: ###### Corollary 1.2 (Cycle-length bound).
L118: 
L119: If $B>3$ is odd and $c_{\max}(B)$ is the largest terminal-cycle length for the four-digit Kaprekar map in base $B$, then we have
L120: 
L121:  | $$c_{\max}(B)\leq\frac{B-1}{2}.$$  |
L122: 
L123: Moreover, equality holds if and only if $B\geq 7$, $B$ is prime, and the least positive solution to $2^{m}\equiv\pm 1\pmod{B}$ is $m=\frac{B-1}{2}$.
L124: ###### Remark.
L125: 
L126: In the edge case $B=5$, one has $c_{\max}(5)=1<2=(B-1)/2$ instead (see [cite26†4 , Lemma 1], or [cite32†8 , §4 and Appendix B]).
L127: 
L128: Thus cite37†Corollary 1.2 gives a universal ceiling and describes exactly when this bound is achieved. We also have the following result:
L129: ###### Corollary 1.3 (Prime bases and maximal cycles).
L130: 
L131: If equality holds in cite37†Corollary 1.2 (so that $B$ is prime), then the number of terminal cycles of length $c_{\max}(B)$ is
L132: 
L133:  | $$\left\lfloor\frac{c_{\max}(B)-1}{2}\right\rfloor.$$  |
L134: ###### Remark.
L135: Our results are a four-digit complement to the broader odd-base theory. Yamagami and Matsui give a detailed theory in base $3$ [cite30†13 ], and Kay and Downes-Ward study fixed points and cycles in odd bases using Kaprekar indices, with regular cycles organized through subgroup and coset data [cite32†8 ]. Their framework treats arbitrary digit-counts and is especially well suited to regular cycles. The present note fixes the digit-count at four.
L136: In this small case, the dynamics are more directly described by the outer and inner digit differences, and after a bounded pre-periodic segment these two differences give a stable region on which the map becomes projective doubling. Therefore, the contribution here is a low-dimensional model that makes the four-digit odd-base dynamics and their cycle counts explicit.
L137: ### Provenance and formal verification
L138: The structural conjectures leading to cite36†Theorem 1.1 and its cycle-length consequences were first formulated by Schwartz and Thakur and communicated to Ono. AxiomProver was then used as an experimental AI-assisted formal mathematics system to produce Lean/mathlib formalizations of the resulting statements. The present paper gives a human-readable account of the mathematics. The formal files, the Lean environment, and the verification protocol are described in cite18†Section 6 .
L139: AxiomProver is credited as a tool rather than as an author, and the human authors take responsibility for the mathematical statements, exposition, attribution, and correctness of the paper.
L140: ### Examples of the main results
L141: 
L142: Here are a few examples that illustrate these results. The cycles are controlled not by decimal accidents, but by the order of $2$ modulo the base, with signs ignored. We start each example with ordinary four-digit strings, and only then pass to the difference and projective coordinates.
L143: ###### Example (The case $B=7$; [cite32†8 , §5]).
L144: 
L145: The sorted four-digit string $3100$ has
L146: 
L147:  | $$d_{1}=3-0=3\qquad\text{and}\qquad d_{2}=1-0=1.$$  |
L148: 
L149: Thus
L150: 
L151:  | $$r=\frac{3+1}{2}=2\qquad\text{and}\qquad s=\frac{3-1}{2}=1.$$  |
L152: 
L153: Writing each iterate as a sorted digit string, the orbit of $3100$ is
L154: 
L155:  | $$3100\longmapsto 5430\longmapsto 5520\longmapsto 5322\longmapsto 5430\longmapsto\dots,$$  |
L156: 
L157: which in difference coordinates is the terminal cycle
L158:  | $$(3,1)\longmapsto(5,1)\longmapsto(5,3)\longmapsto(3,1).$$  |
L159: 
L160: Here $(B-1)/2=3$, and $2$ has projective order $3$ modulo $7$, so the largest four-digit Kaprekar cycles have length $3$. This agrees with the count $\lfloor(3-1)/2\rfloor=1$.
L161: ###### Example (The case $B=11$).
L162: 
L163: The sorted four-digit string $5100$ has $(d_{1},d_{2})=(5,1)$, and hence
L164: 
L165:  | $$r=3\qquad\text{and}\qquad s=2.$$  |
L166: 
L167: Writing each iterate as a sorted digit string, the orbit of $5100$ is
L168: 
L169:  | $$5100\longmapsto 9650\longmapsto 9920\longmapsto 9632\longmapsto 7742\longmapsto 7652\longmapsto 9650\longmapsto\dots.$$  |
L170: 
L171: In difference coordinates this is the terminal cycle
L172: 
L173:  | $$(5,1)\to(9,1)\to(9,7)\to(7,3)\to(5,3)\to(5,1).$$  |
L174: Since $2^{5}\equiv-1\pmod{11}$ and no smaller positive power of $2$ is congruent to $\pm 1$, we have $c_{\max}(11)=5$. There are
L175: 
L176:  | $$\left\lfloor\frac{5-1}{2}\right\rfloor=2$$  |
L177: 
L178: cycles of length five; the other one is
L179: 
L180:  | $$(3,1)\to(9,5)\to(7,1)\to(9,3)\to(7,5)\to(3,1).$$  |
L181: ###### Example (The case $B=9$).
L182: 
L183: The composite base $B=9$ shows why the inequality is usually strict. Starting from the sorted string $5100$, we have $(d_{1},d_{2})=(5,1)$ and $(r,s)=(3,2)$. The terminal behavior in difference coordinates is
L184: 
L185:  | $$(5,1)\to(7,1)\to(7,5)\to(5,1),$$  |
L186: 
L187: with the second cycle
L188: 
L189:  | $$(3,1)\to(7,3)\to(5,3)\to(3,1).$$  |
L190: 
L191: Here $(B-1)/2=4$, but $2^{3}\equiv-1\pmod{9}$, so the terminal cycles have length $3$, not $4$.
L192: ###### Example (The case $B=17$).
L193: 
L194: Finally, a prime base need not give equality. For $B=17$, the sorted four-digit string $5100$ again has $(d_{1},d_{2})=(5,1)$ and $(r,s)=(3,2)$, but $2^{4}\equiv-1\pmod{17}$. Thus the largest terminal cycles have length $4$, not $(17-1)/2=8$.
L195: The rest of the paper is organized as follows. cite10†Section 2 introduces the difference coordinates and proves that every orbit reaches the stable odd region after at most three steps. cite13†Section 3 identifies the hidden projective coordinates and proves that, on this region, one Kaprekar step is just doubling in those coordinates. cite14†Section 4 translates the projective model into explicit cycle-count formulas, and then deduces the general cycle-length bound and the prime-base obstruction to equality.
L196: cite15†Section 5 treats prime bases in detail and counts the largest cycles when the bound is attained. cite18†Section 6 describes the accompanying Lean/mathlib formalization, including the AxiomProver protocol, the formal files, and the verification environment.
L197: ### Acknowledgments
L198: 
L199: The authors thank Rubén Ballester and Andrew Granville for helpful comments regarding this project, and Granville in particular for suggesting promising directions for future work that generalize these results. We also thank the editors of the Journal of Integer Sequences and the anonymous referee for helpful comments and suggestions, including the suggestion to provide the examples $B=9$ and $B=63$ in cite14†Section 4 .
L200: ## 2. Difference coordinates for four digits
L201: 
L202: We now turn from the statement of the result to the mechanism behind it. The first step is to reduce the digit operation to a map on two integers.
L203: ### 2.1. Difference coordinates
L204: 
L205: Fix an odd base $B>3$. Let
L206: 
L207:  | $$\overrightarrow{N}=[a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}]\qquad\text{with}\qquad a_{1}\geq a_{2}\geq a_{3}\geq a_{4}$$  |
L208: 
L209: be the decreasing rearrangement of a four-digit string. We ignore constant strings, since they map to zero. As in (cite38†1 ), let $d_{1}\coloneq a_{1}-a_{4}$ and $d_{2}\coloneq a_{2}-a_{3}$ so that
L210: 
L211:  | $$1\leq d_{1}<B\qquad\text{and}\qquad 0\leq d_{2}\leq d_{1}.$$  |
L212: Then Kaprekar subtraction depends only on $(d_{1},d_{2})$, as in [cite26†4 ]. Indeed,
L213: 
L214:  |  | $\displaystyle(a_{1}B^{3}+a_{2}B^{2}+a_{3}B+a_{4})-(a_{4}B^{3}+a_{3}B^{2}+a_{2}B+a_{1})$  |
L215:  |  | $\displaystyle=d_{1}(B^{3}-1)+d_{2}(B^{2}-B).$  |
L216: 
L217: Thus the future orbit after one step is determined by the pair $(d_{1},d_{2})$.
L218: 
L219: If $d_{2}>0$, ordinary base-$B$ subtraction gives the unsorted output digits
L220: 
L221: (5)  |  | $$[d_{1},\ d_{2}-1,\ B-d_{2}-1,\ B-d_{1}].$$  |
L222: If $d_{2}=0$, the subtraction has one more borrow, and the unsorted output digits are
L223: 
L224: (6)  |  | $$[d_{1}-1,\ B-1,\ B-1,\ B-d_{1}].$$  |
L225: Let $K_{B}$ denote the induced map on $X_{B}$ as defined in (cite39†2 ). To compute $K_{B}(d_{1},d_{2})$, one sorts the four entries in (cite40†5 ) or (cite41†6 ) in decreasing order and then takes the outer and inner differences. This passage to difference coordinates does not lose eventual cycle lengths.
L226: Indeed, a digit-level orbit determines a difference-coordinate orbit, and conversely a periodic orbit in difference coordinates lifts to a digit-level periodic orbit by the subtraction formulas (cite40†5 ) and (cite41†6 ). If two digit strings in such a lifted orbit were equal, their difference pairs would also be equal, so the period is the same. Thus it is enough to count terminal cycles for $K_{B}$ on $X_{B}$.
L227: ### 2.2. Escaping the pre-period
L228: 
L229: The rest of this section is a cleanup step. We show that the boundary phenomena disappear after a bounded number of iterations, leaving a simple stable region on which the projective model will live.
L230: ###### Lemma 2.1 (Pre-period into the stable odd region).
L231: 
L232: For every odd $B>3$,
L233: 
L234:  | $$K_{B}^{3}(X_{B})\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{B}.$$  |
L235: 
L236: Moreover $\mathcal{T}_{B}$ is forward invariant under $K_{B}$.
L237: 
L238: The proof of cite42†Lemma 2.1 is divided into a few cases resolved via explicit calculation of $K_{B}$. This calculation also appears in [cite26†4 , equations (1.1)–(1.3)], and [cite29†2 , §2], although our organization of the cases is slightly different.
L239: ###### Case 2.1.1.
L240: 
L241: cite42†Lemma 2.1 holds in the case $d_{1}>d_{2}>0$. In fact:
L242: 
L243:   * •
L244: 
L245: If $d_{1}>d_{2}>0$ and $d_{1}\equiv d_{2}\pmod{2}$, then $K_{B}(d_{1},d_{2})\in\mathcal{T}_{B}$.
L246: 
L247:   * •
L248: 
L249: If $d_{1}>d_{2}>0$ but $d_{1}\not\equiv d_{2}\pmod{2}$, then $K_{B}^{2}(d_{1},d_{2})\in\mathcal{T}_{B}$.
L250: ###### Proof for cite43†Case 2.1.1 .
L251: 
L252: Abbreviate the four entries in (cite40†5 ) by
L253: 
L254:  | $$A\coloneq d_{1}\qquad\text{and}\qquad C\coloneq d_{2}-1\qquad\text{and}\qquad D\coloneq B-d_{2}-1\qquad\text{and}\qquad E\coloneq B-d_{1}.$$  |
L255: We always have $A>C$ and $D\geq E$; also $A\neq E$ and $C\neq D$. We note the case $D>A>C>E$ is also impossible, because this case would require both $d_{1}+d_{2}<B-1$ and $d_{1}+d_{2}>B+1$. Hence, we must be in one of the five situations listed in cite44†Table 1 . Of course, only rows whose displayed differences are nonnegative can actually occur.
L256:  | $$\begin{array}[]{ccc}\hline\cr\text{Ordering}&K_{B}(d_{1},d_{2})&\text{In $\mathcal{T}_{B}$?}\\
L257: \hline\cr A\geq D\geq E\geq C&(d_{1}-d_{2}+1,\ d_{1}-d_{2}-1)&\text{Iff }d_{1}\equiv d_{2}\bmod 2\\
L258: D\geq E>A>C&(B-2d_{2},\ B-2d_{1})&\text{Always}\\
L259: A\geq D>C\geq E&(2d_{1}-B,\ B-2d_{2})&\text{Always}\\
L260: D\geq A>E\geq C&(B-2d_{2},\ 2d_{1}-B)&\text{Always}\\
L261: A>C>D\geq E&(2d_{1}-B,\ 2d_{2}-B)&\text{Always}\\
L262: \hline\cr\end{array}$$  |
L263: Table 1. Possible results of $K_{B}(d_{1},d_{2})$ when $d_{1}>d_{2}>0$.
L264: We assert the last four rows of cite44†Table 1 always lie in $\mathcal{T}_{B}$. Indeed, it is clear the entries are odd. Moreover, they are easily seen to be unequal; in the third row we have $C\geq E\implies d_{1}+d_{2}\geq B+1$ while in the fourth row we have $D\geq A\implies d_{1}+d_{2}\leq B-1$. Hence in the third and fourth row $d_{1}+d_{2}\neq B$ always holds and the two entries are unequal.
L265: It remains to only deal with the first row, which lies in $\mathcal{T}_{B}$ exactly when $d_{1}\equiv d_{2}\pmod{2}$. It suffices to show that
L266: 
L267: (7)  |  | $$K_{B}(h+1,h-1)\in\mathcal{T}_{B}\quad\text{for each odd}\quad h\geq 1.$$  |
L268: 
L269: Indeed (cite45†7 ) can be checked directly:
L270: 
L271:   * •
L272: 
L273: If $h\neq 1$, we apply cite44†Table 1 a second time to the new pair $(h+1,h-1)$. For $(h+1,h-1)$, all five rows of cite44†Table 1 are in $\mathcal{T}_{B}$ and we are done.
L274: 
L275:   * •
L276: If $h=1$ then in fact $(h+1,h-1)=(2,0)$. Although cite44†Table 1 does not apply, we can directly compute
L277: 
L278:  | $$K_{B}(2,0)=(B-2,1)\in\mathcal{T}_{B}.\qed$$  |
